source: US Geological Survey Mineral Commodity Summaries (rounded); refining from IEA and company reports
caveat: Rounded and approximate. Output is published by country, not by mine, so the glow by region is an estimate. Refining is much more concentrated than mining: China does roughly 90% of it. Projects can change quickly.
uses: Rare earths are 17 metals that go into the strongest magnets (electric cars, wind turbines, phones, drones, jets and missiles), plus lasers, catalysts and glass.

fields.note: The world's biggest rare earth mine, mostly the 'light' elements used in magnets.

fields.n: Southern ionic clays (Jiangxi, Guangdong, Fujian, China)
fields.note: Clay deposits rich in the scarcer 'heavy' elements (dysprosium, terbium).
Second main source of light rare earths in China.
Heavy rare earths dug from clay, mostly small mines, nearly all sent on to China for refining.
The main US mine. Its ore has long been sent to China for refining, though US refining and magnet plants are being built.
A very rich deposit; the main source outside China and the US.
Small-scale mining, mostly as a by-product.
Rare earths in monazite sand, a by-product of mineral sands mining.
Monazite from mineral sands and clay deposits.

sites.note: China's rare earth capital: refines Bayan Obo ore and makes many of the world's magnets.
Hub for the heavy rare earths and magnets.
Lynas separation plant, the biggest refining site outside China.
Lynas plant that cracks and leaches Mount Weld concentrate before it is shipped on.
Separation and metals plant, one of the few in Europe.
